column1: State the Euthyphro dilemma and what it targets.
column2: Socrates asks Euthyphro (Euthyphro 10a): is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because the gods love it? If the first, piety is a standard independent of divine will — the gods recognize goodness, they do not create it. If the second, piety is arbitrary: anything the gods happened to love would count as pious, and 'good' adds nothing beyond 'loved by the gods.' The dilemma survives the dialogue's failure to define piety and remains the standing objection to divine-command theories of morality: they must take one horn or the other.

column1: Reconstruct the Laws' argument in the Crito: why must Socrates not escape?
column2: The personified Laws argue (Crito 50a-54d): Socrates has lived seventy years under Athens' laws, benefiting from them and raising children under them; staying was an agreement to obey or persuade. To break a verdict he dislikes would destroy the laws' authority as such — a private citizen cannot pick which judgments stand. Escape would also harm his friends and confirm the jury's picture of him. Note the tension the dialogue leaves standing: the Apology (29c-d) promises disobedience to any order to stop philosophizing. Obey-or-persuade governs verdicts; it does not obviously govern commands to act unjustly.

column1: What is the elenchus, and what does it establish?
column2: The elenchus is Socrates' method in the early dialogues: take an interlocutor's proposed definition ('piety is what the gods love'), draw out its consequences through short agreed steps, and show it contradicts other beliefs the interlocutor holds more firmly. Its results are characteristically negative — definitions fall, dialogues end in aporia. What it establishes, at minimum, is inconsistency in the examined person's beliefs and the exposure of false conceit of knowledge. Whether it can establish positive doctrine — and if so, how — is disputed; the constructive use Plato later makes of Socratic questioning presupposes an answer the early dialogues never state.

column1: Define Socratic ignorance and the doctrine that virtue is knowledge.
column2: Socratic ignorance (Apology 21d, 23a-b): Socrates' one epistemic advantage is knowing that he does not know what he does not know — human wisdom, against the craftsmen's and politicians' double ignorance of not knowing and thinking they know. Virtue is knowledge is its ethical twin: if virtue is knowledge of good and bad, no one who possesses it can fail to act on it, so no one does wrong willingly — wrongdoing is ignorance, and the remedy is examination, not punishment. The doctrine drives the Meno's recollection and the Gorgias' paradoxes, and its hard case is akrasia: knowing better and doing worse.

column1: What is the Socrates problem?
column2: A scholarly framing, contested as such: Plato's Socrates changes across the dialogues. In the early works (Apology, Crito, Euthyphro) he practices the elenchus, professes ignorance, and holds ethical doctrines only. In middle works (Phaedo, Republic, Symposium) he expounds Forms, immortality, and a political system the historical Socrates probably never held. The developmentalist reading treats the early dialogues as closest to the historical Socrates and the rest as Plato's own philosophy in his teacher's mouth; unitarians resist extracting an evolution from dramatic works. Every attribution of a doctrine 'to Socrates' or 'to Plato' silently takes a side — take yours knowingly.

column1: What is a Form (eidos)?
column2: A Form is an eternal, changeless, mind-independent pattern that sensible particulars imperfectly instantiate: Beauty itself, Equality itself, Justice itself. Particulars are many, unstable, and deficient — no two sticks are perfectly equal, no sensible beautiful thing is beautiful in every respect, at every time, to every observer. The Form is the single stable standard by which such things are judged and are what they are. Strict knowledge (episteme) is of Forms; of the shifting sensible world there is only belief. Forms are not shinier physical objects located somewhere: Plato's spatial language for them is metaphorical, and treating it literally is the entry-level misreading.

column1: Reconstruct the recollection argument from the Meno's slave-boy scene.
column2: Meno's paradox (80d): you cannot search for what you do not know — you would not recognize it if found — nor for what you know already. Socrates questions an enslaved boy with no geometry teaching and, by questions and diagrams alone, leads him to double the square (82b-85b). Conclusion: the boy recovered the truth from within himself; learning is recollection (anamnesis) of what the soul knew before birth. The standing objection: the questions are artfully leading — Socrates draws the figures and orders every step — so the scene may show guided invention rather than recovery. The argument needs the stronger claim, and the text knows it.

column1: Reconstruct the Phaedo's recollection argument from equals.
column2: We perceive equal sticks and stones, and judge them deficient — they strive to be like Equality itself but fall short (Phaedo 74a-75b). But we could not judge them deficient against a standard the senses never supplied: no sensible equal is perfectly equal. We must therefore have known Equality itself before birth, and forgotten it at birth; perceiving equals reminds us of it. Conclusion: the soul existed, and knew the Forms, before it was embodied — Plato's bridge from epistemology to the soul's pre-existence, and the premise the Phaedo's immortality arguments then build on. Its most pressed point: why the standard must be known before, rather than formed by abstraction.

column1: Reconstruct the Phaedo's final argument for immortality (105b-107a).
column2: The last and strongest of the Phaedo's arguments turns on causation by Forms. Soul is essentially the bearer of life to whatever body it occupies. What essentially brings a characteristic cannot admit that characteristic's opposite: fire, bringing heat, cannot admit cold; snow, bringing cold, cannot admit heat; three cannot admit evenness. Soul brings life; death is life's opposite; therefore soul cannot admit death — it is deathless (athanaton), and what is deathless is indestructible. The argument's strength is that it rests on what soul is, not on cycles or resemblances. Its exposure is the same: everything rides on the essentialist premise.

column1: State Simmias' and Cebes' objections in the Phaedo, and how Socrates answers.
column2: Simmias (85e-88c): the soul may be like a harmony of the lyre — real, invisible, but a byproduct of bodily attunement, destroyed when the instrument breaks. Socrates answers via recollection: the soul pre-exists the body, but a harmony cannot pre-exist the elements it harmonizes; harmony also admits degrees, soul does not. Cebes (87a-88c): grant pre-existence — a weaver outlives many cloaks yet wears out in the end; why should the soul not wear out across many lives? This is the objection the final argument (105b-107a) exists to meet: it must show not longevity but deathlessness by essence.

column1: What is anamnesis?
column2: Anamnesis is Plato's doctrine that learning is recollection: the soul is immortal, knew the Forms before birth, and forgot them in being born; experience occasions recovery of what it already possesses. It does double duty. Epistemologically (Meno) it answers the paradox of inquiry — you can search for what you do not consciously know because you latently know it. Psychologically and religiously (Phaedo) it is evidence for the soul's pre-existence and a premise toward immortality. You need not accept literal pre-existence to see the move: some knowledge, Plato insists, cannot come from sense experience alone, because experience presupposes standards — equality, likeness, number — it does not supply.

column1: What is participation (methexis)?
column2: Participation is Plato's name for the relation between a particular and its Form: a beautiful thing is beautiful by participating in Beauty itself; equal sticks participate in Equality. It is the load-bearing joint of the whole theory — and its least explained part. Plato uses several models (presence, sharing, imitation of a paradigm) without settling the mechanism, and the Parmenides presses the vagueness hard: does the particular partake of the whole Form or a part of it, and is the Form then divided among its participants? Aristotle's verdict stands as the standard objection: to say particulars participate in Forms is, he charges, to speak in poetic metaphors rather than explanations.

column1: Distinguish doxa from episteme, and say what hangs on it.
column2: Doxa is belief or opinion: cognition directed at the sensible world of becoming — things that are and are not, that appear differently from different standpoints. Episteme is knowledge: cognition of what fully is, the Forms, stable and the same in every respect (Republic V, 475e-480a). The distinction is not between false and true beliefs — a true opinion about a road can guide you as well as knowledge (Meno 97a-b) — but between cognition that can give an account of its object and cognition that cannot. It grounds the philosopher's claim to rule: only episteme grasps what justice and the good are.

column1: Set out Glaucon's challenge and the Ring of Gyges (Republic II).
column2: Glaucon restates Thrasymachus at full strength (357a-362c). Goods divide into three classes: good in themselves alone; good both in themselves and for their consequences; and good for their consequences alone. Justice must be shown in the second, finest class — good in itself, not merely for its rewards. The Ring of Gyges (359c-360d): an invisibility ring lets a shepherd seduce the queen, kill the king, take the throne. Anyone, Glaucon claims, would do the same; we are just only because we cannot be unjust with impunity. Adeimantus adds that praises of justice praise its reputation. The remaining nine books answer: justice as the soul's health, worth having with consequences stripped.

column1: Reconstruct the tripartite division argument (Republic IV).
column2: By the principle of opposites (436b), the same thing cannot do or suffer opposites at the same time, in the same respect, toward the same object. A thirsty person desires drink (appetite urges acceptance) and at the same time refuses it (something forbids) — opposed pulls toward one object cannot come from an undifferentiated soul, so appetite and reason are distinct (439a-d). Spirit is a third source: Leontius grows angry at his own desire to stare at corpses — anger at appetite, allied with reason (439e-440a). Conclusion: at least three functionally distinct sources of motivation. The live debate: functional sources, established; literal parts, each a mini-agent, not obviously.

column1: Give the tripartite soul's parts, their objects, and the definition of justice built on them.
column2: Reason seeks truth and the good of the whole soul; spirit seeks honor, victory, and standing — it is anger, shame, and competitiveness; appetite seeks bodily satisfaction and money, its enabler. In the just soul reason rules, spirit assists, appetite obeys; in the city, rulers, auxiliaries, and producers correspond. Justice in both is the same condition: each part (or class) doing its own work and not meddling in the others' (433a-434d, 443c-444e). Injustice is internal civil war. Hence the just person acts justly outwardly because their soul is ordered — justice is psychological health, not compliance with a list of acts.

column1: Reconstruct the philosopher-king argument.
column2: Ruling well requires knowledge of the Good — of what justice and benefit actually are, not how they appear (Republic V-VI). Such knowledge is possible but rare, attained only by the philosophical nature after decades of mathematical and dialectical education. Therefore evils will not cease for cities until philosophers rule as kings or kings philosophize (473c-d) — the third and greatest of Book V's waves. The rulers must then be compelled to return to the cave and govern (519c-521b): they would rather contemplate, and the reluctance is itself a qualification — anyone who wants the office wants the wrong thing. Critics ask whether knowledge licenses rule over the unconsenting.

column1: Name the three waves of Republic V and which is greatest.
column2: Book V's three 'waves' of paradox (449a-480a): first, women of guardian nature receive the same education and duties as men, warfare included — sex is relevant to childbearing, not to guardianship (451c-457b). Second, wives and children are held in common among the guardians, mating arranged by the rulers, so no private family divides a guardian's loyalty from the city (457c-466d). Third and greatest (473c-d): philosophers must become kings, or kings philosophers, or cities will never rest from evils. Each wave applies the founding principle harder: each person does the one work their nature fits them for, and nothing private competes with that assignment.

column1: What is the noble lie, and what is it for?
column2: The noble lie (Republic III, 414b-415d) is a myth Socrates proposes telling the city: citizens were formed inside the earth, are all brothers born of one mother, but have metals mixed in their souls — gold in rulers, silver in auxiliaries, bronze and iron in producers. Its purposes are loyalty (all citizens are kin, the city their common mother) and acceptance of class as natural rather than imposed. Readers divide: propaganda licensing rulers to deceive; a civic myth whose content — worth is nature, not birth — cuts against hereditary aristocracy; or a proposal Socrates is visibly ashamed to utter. Present the disagreement; the text supports each in part.

column1: Reconstruct the function (ergon) argument of Republic I.
column2: Everything has a function it alone performs, or performs best: eyes see, a pruning knife cuts; a thing performs its function well through its own excellence, arete, and badly through its defect (352d-353b). The soul's functions are living, managing, deliberating, and ruling. The soul's excellence is justice — the premise Thrasymachus is maneuvered into granting. Therefore the just soul performs its function well, lives well, and living well is happiness: the just life is happier than the unjust (353a-354a). Socrates himself flags the result as premature — they feasted before the main course (354a-c) — and Book II reopens the whole question on harder terms.

column1: Give the Cave as an epistemological argument, not a summary.
column2: Prisoners chained take shadows for reality (Republic VII, 514a-517a). As argument: (1) cognition formed from appearances mistakes the appearance-order for the world — the prisoners are not stupid, they are us with our evidence restricted. (2) Correction is not new information but reorientation: education turns the soul from becoming toward being (518b-d), painfully and by stages, as vision adjusts. (3) The one who has ascended owes a return: knowledge of the Good obliges rule in the cave (519c-521b). The standing objection: the freed prisoner's 'outside' may be another cave — how is the ascent verified from inside? Plato's answer must be the Line's hierarchy of cognition, not the story itself.

column1: What is the Form of the Good, and what work does the Sun analogy do?
column2: The Good is the highest Form in the Republic's metaphysics: the source of intelligibility and of being to the Forms, itself 'beyond being' in dignity and power (509b). Socrates declines to define it directly (506d-e) and gives the Sun as its offspring in the visible realm: as the sun makes visible things visible and gives them generation and growth, the Good makes intelligible things knowable and gives them being. The analogy supplies structural role, not content — the Good is the condition under which knowledge and its objects are possible at all. Whether that is profundity or metaphor doing metaphysics' work is the standing objection, and Plato stages it knowingly.

column1: Lay out the Divided Line's four segments (Republic VI, 509d-511e).
column2: The Line divides cognition by its objects, in ascending order. 1. Eikasia, imagination: images, shadows, reflections. 2. Pistis, belief: physical objects themselves. These two are doxa, opinion, directed at the visible. 3. Dianoia, thought: mathematical objects, reasoned from hypotheses with the help of diagrams — the geometer draws a triangle but reasons about Triangularity. 4. Noesis, understanding: the Forms themselves, grasped by dialectic, which treats hypotheses as stepping stones to an unhypothetical first principle, the Good. The Line is the Cave drawn as a diagram: same ascent, two notations. Its proportions encode a claim — clarity of cognition tracks reality of object.

column1: Reconstruct the Book X argument that imitation is twice removed from truth.
column2: Three levels (Republic X, 596a-598b): the Form of Bed; the carpenter's bed, made looking to the Form; the painter's bed, made copying the carpenter's bed as it appears from one angle. The painter's product is therefore twice removed from truth, and the imitator knows neither the craft nor the use of what he depicts — the painter of a bridle knows neither bridle-making nor horsemanship (598b-602b). Poetry adds a charge: it feeds the soul's inferior part, indulging grief and laughter we restrain in life (605a-606d). The ban is qualified, not total: hymns and encomia are admitted, and poetry may return if it can defend itself in argument (607a-608b).

column1: State the Third Man regress and the standard reply.
column2: Plato raises it against himself (Parmenides 132a-b). If many large things are large by participating in the Form Largeness, and the Form is large, then particulars plus Form form a set of large things needing a further Form to explain their likeness — and so on infinitely; the theory generates the multitude it was meant to explain. The standard reply: the regress needs two assumptions — self-predication (the Form is an instance of what it names) and non-identity (the Form is distinct from its instances). Qualify either and the regress halts: participation is not resemblance between two things of a kind. Which assumption Plato would surrender is genuinely disputed.

column1: What does the Myth of Er claim, and where does it leave responsibility?
column2: Er, killed in battle, revives on his pyre and reports the afterlife (Republic X, 614b-621d): souls are judged, rewarded or punished, then choose their next lives from lots spread before them — the first soul, careless from habit, chooses a tyranny and laments. Lachesis' spokesman states the moral: 'The blame is his who chooses; god is blameless' (617e). Cosmic justice thus preserves responsibility inside necessity: your lot determines which lives are offered, not which you pick, and philosophy is the education that teaches choosing well. Plato ends the Republic by relocating justice's payoff: in this life as psychic order, beyond it as the chooser's own doing.

column1: Reconstruct the Gorgias argument that rhetoric is flattery, not a craft.
column2: Socrates distinguishes crafts from knacks (Gorgias 462b-466a). A craft (techne) aims at its object's good and can give an account of itself: medicine for the body, legislation and justice for the soul. Flattery guesses at pleasure without knowledge of the good, and divides into counterfeits of each craft: cookery counterfeits medicine, cosmetics gymnastics, sophistry legislation — and rhetoric counterfeits justice. Rhetoric : justice :: pastry-baking : medicine: it produces the appearance of health while the condition worsens. Its power in courtrooms and assemblies is the power to gratify, not to improve — and the orator who cannot say what justice is cannot claim to practice an art of it.

column1: Reconstruct the Gorgias argument that doing injustice is worse than suffering it.
column2: Against Polus (Gorgias 469b-479e): doing injustice is more shameful than suffering it, and the more shameful is either more painful or worse; it is not more painful, so it is worse for the doer. Punishment enters as medicine: punishment releases the soul from its worst condition, injustice, as medicine releases the body from disease. The happiest unjust man is not the one who escapes detection but the one who is caught and cured; the tyrant Archelaus, Polus' exhibit, is the most miserable man. The premise modern readers refuse first: that punishment benefits the punished. Refuse it, and the medical analogy — not the shame argument — is what falls.

column1: Define eros and climb Diotima's ladder (Symposium 210a-212a).
column2: Eros, in Diotima's teaching, is desire for good and immortality through generation in beauty — neither god nor mortal but a daimon in between, philosophy's portrait (202a-204b). The ladder: love of one beautiful body; recognition that beauty in all bodies is one, so the lover relaxes his grip on the instance; beauty of souls valued above bodies; beauty in laws and practices; in the sciences and knowledge; until he catches sight of Beauty itself — eternal, unmixed, not beautiful in one respect and ugly in another. Nussbaum's objection: the individual beloved becomes a rung and is discarded. Sheffield's reply: the ascent enlarges eros's objects; it does not abandon them.

column1: What is dialectic, for Plato?
column2: Dialectic is the capstone method of the Republic's education (531d-535a): the discipline that, unlike mathematics, does not rest in its hypotheses but uses them as stepping stones, destroying them as mere assumptions, until it reaches the unhypothetical first principle — the Good — and can give and receive an account of the being of each thing. In the middle dialogues it names reason's ascent from images to Forms; in the late dialogues (Sophist, Statesman) it becomes collection and division: carving kinds at their natural joints. Across both, dialectic is philosophy's self-image: not the possession of conclusions but the practiced ability to survive questioning about them.

column1: Show why the Theaetetus's three definitions of knowledge fail.
column2: First: knowledge is perception (151e). Protagoras' measure-doctrine and the flux theory support it; it collapses at 184b-186e — being, sameness, and number are grasped by the soul itself through no organ, and knowledge lies in reasoning about the given, not in the giving. Second: knowledge is true belief (187b). False belief becomes inexplicable — the wax tablet (191c-196c) and aviary (197a-200c) model error as mismatching or misgrasping, but neither covers error in pure thought. Third: true belief with an account, logos (201c-210b). Each sense of logos either repeats the belief, lists elements without unity, or adds only a distinguishing mark anyone might have. The dialogue ends in aporia — deliberately.

column1: What is separation (chorismos), and why does it matter?
column2: Separation is the thesis that Forms exist apart from their sensible participants — Equality itself is not any equal thing, nor in them. It secures the theory's claims: a standard that is another instance could not arbitrate among instances. It also generates the theory's deepest problems: how a changeless, separate Form relates to a changing particular (participation becomes obscure), and Aristotle's objection — separate Forms double the world without explaining it, when what was wanted was the form in things. Nearly every later theory of universals is a position on this one decision: separate, immanent, or nominal. Plato's late dialogues worry at it; Aristotle rebuilds metaphysics by refusing it.

column1: State the developmentalist and unitarian readings of Plato. CONTESTED.
column2: CONTESTED — presented as a dispute, not a result. Developmentalists read the dialogues as an evolution: an early Socratic period (elenchus, ethical definitions), a middle period of Plato's system (Forms, immortality, the Republic), and a late critical period (Parmenides, Sophist) revising that system. Their evidence: stylometry (statistical analysis of the Greek) clusters a late group, and doctrines visibly shift. Unitarians reply that the dialogues are unified works whose differences are of speaker, audience, and purpose, not of belief — extracting doctrine's biography from them mistakes literature for a diary. Most scholars work developmentally about chronology while hedging about doctrine; the dossier flags the dispute wherever an attribution depends on it.

column1: What happens to the Forms in the late dialogues? CONTESTED.
column2: CONTESTED — the texts are fixed; what Plato concluded from them is not. In the Parmenides, Plato has the young Socrates' theory dismantled by Parmenides himself: participation dilemmas, the Third Man, and the 'greatest difficulty' — if Forms are separate, gods could not know our world nor we theirs (133a-134e). In the Sophist, the Eleatic Stranger has Forms blend and communicate, rethinks being and non-being, and the separation of the middle period looks revised. Developmentalists read abandonment or major revision; unitarians read refinement of a theory never as crude as its critics' version; a third line reads the Parmenides as training exercise. The dossier presents all three and settles none.
